extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians and comedy writers (especially quiet performers and those mining anxiety material)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft rules for performing and writing quiet-voiced stand-up, with specific advice on using anxiety as material, avoiding self-deprecation traps, testing premises on Twitter, and reading audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke survive at low volume?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke survive at low volume?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quiet voice is a deliberate choice that forces the audience to lean in; the audience's attention becomes the joke's amplification. Downsides: the room must be small or you're fighting acoustics. The quiet comic's bomb is also quiet — the audience just looks confused. Practice reading whether silence is engagement or disengagement; count how many people are LOOKING at you, not just listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is anxiety material specific to a micro-ritual?
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxiety material works best when it's specific to a SPECIFIC SITUATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "I have anxiety" is not material. "I rehearsed leaving the elevator" is material. The audience laughs at recognition of micro-rituals, not at diagnosis. Use concrete, narrowly-observed behaviors or rituals as the premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have you balanced self-deprecation with sincere observation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you balanced self-deprecation with sincere observation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-deprecation can become a flinch; audiences tire of it and comics can get stuck in that persona. The recommended cure is to allow yourself ONE clear, sincere observation per set that you stand behind, alongside any self-deprecating material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have you tested the premise in writing first?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you tested the premise in writing first?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter is a free open mic. Use short-form writing to test premises before relying on them onstage. Numbers (likes, retweets) approximate stage laughter — imperfectly — but are useful signals to iterate and refine premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are you reading engagement, not just laughter?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you reading engagement, not just laughter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond counting laughs, observe whether the room is visually engaged (who is looking at you). For quiet material, silence can be either focused attention or disengagement — the performer must learn to distinguish and respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are you commanding silence, or being abandoned to it?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you commanding silence, or being abandoned to it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deliberate quiet moment can work if the performer is commanding it; if the audience simply stops engaging, the moment fails. Practice reading body language and eye contact to tell which it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and acoustics suitability for quiet material
rubrics_metrics.description: The room must be small or you're fighting acoustics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quiet delivery requires venues where subtle vocal choices register; large rooms or poor acoustics will erase the effect. Choose appropriately sized rooms, manage microphones, or adapt volume/style to the space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Twitter as a joke workshop
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter is a free open mic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat tweets as tests of premise and wording. Social metrics approximate stage reaction and can help refine timing and punch. Don't mistake tweet performance for final stage craft—use the platform to iterate premises and phrasing.
